title: Why Intimidation Is A Terrible Classroom Management Strategy nagement-strategy/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin condemns intimidation — glaring, threatening, yelling, scolding, browbeating — as a classroom management method, arguing that any amount of it crosses a line, even when used only occasionally or with certain students. He lists its costs: it's hurtful, unnecessary given better available skills, personally stressful for the teacher, and fills the room with palpable tension. It also destroys trust and rapport by essentially breaking the teacher's word to follow their classroom management plan, sabotages healthy accountability by keeping students angry rather than reflective, and risks parent complaints that damage a teacher's reputation. He acknowledges intimidation can produce short-term compliance but insists it undermines long-term classroom management. The piece ends bluntly, labeling anyone who purposely uses power to force compliance through fear a 'bully.'
points: Any amount of intimidation, even occasional or limited to certain students, crosses a line and is fundamentally hurtful.
Intimidation is unnecessary because effective, non-fear-based classroom management skills can be learned with practice.
Using intimidation is itself highly stressful for the teacher, filling them with guilt and perpetual conflict.
Intimidation sabotages healthy accountability because angry, resentful students can't reflect calmly on their misbehavior.
Reliance on intimidation risks parent complaints and reputational damage, and is ultimately labeled bullying.
quotes: Glaring, threatening, yelling, scolding, browbeating, pressuring, overbearing . . . few teachers would admit to using intimidation as a classroom management method, even to themselves.
Whenever fear enters the equation, to any degree, it’s hurtful to students.
Using intimidation is remarkably stressful—filling you with apprehension, weighing you down with often-unrecognized guilt, and causing you to be in a state of perpetual conflict with your students.
Most teachers who resort to hurtful methods like intimidation do so in lieu of following their classroom management plan—which amounts to going back on their word.
The use of intimidation doesn’t allow students to reflect on their misbehavior because they’re too busy boiling with anger at their teacher.
But there is a name for those who purposely use their position of power or authority to force others to do what they want: Bully.
